projectDesc.p: Encoded for the Experiencing War web site for the Veterans History Project.

samplingDecl.p: The recording of the interview with Sam Edward Buemi was digitized.

editorialDecl.p: This transcription was encoded with minimal changes to the original text in an effort to preserve original content and idiosyncrasies of the person interviewed. Period language and terminology are also retained. Encoding is literal with regard to the transcriptionist's capitalization, punctuation, and spelling. Spelling errors are indicated with [sic]; however, recurring errors in spelling within a single document have been marked the first time and not subsequently.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: This is the oral history of World War II veteran, Sam Edward Buemi, who goes by the name of Bill. Mr. Buemi served in the U.S. Army with the 9th and 3rd Infantry Divisions. He served in Africa, Sicily and Italy and his highest rank was staff sergeant. I'm Tom Swope and this recording was made at Mr. Buemi's home in Lyndhurst, Ohio on August 26th, 2003. Bill was 83 at the time of this recording. Where were you living in 1941?

sp.speaker: Sam Edward Buemi
sp.p: 61st and Woodland.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Sam Edward Buemi
sp.p: That's a bad neighborhood now. I mean, you know, but --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: How old were you then in '41?

sp.speaker: Sam Edward Buemi
sp.p: Be twenty -- I'm 83 now.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: So let's see --

sp.speaker: Sam Edward Buemi
sp.p: Must be about 22 then, 23.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: So you probably were working at the time in '41?

sp.speaker: Sam Edward Buemi
sp.p: Oh, yeah.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Do you have specific memories of December 7th, '41?

sp.speaker: Sam Edward Buemi
sp.p: Yeah. I figured, well, I had a few problems when I was younger. I figured, well, I'd take a little vacation cause I listened to Gabriel Heater, right. This guy says, Well, listen, the war won't last 30, 60 -- 60 days or something. I figured, well, let me get the hell out of here and take a vacation, you know. So when they called me to go, I was glad to get out of here, you know. And never knowing it was going to last four years.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: So did you sign up or did you take voluntary election?

sp.speaker: Sam Edward Buemi
sp.p: No, no. They -- I was drafted.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Sam Edward Buemi
sp.p: No. And like I say, I was glad to get away from everybody, you know, just like starting life anew, get out of here. But my first impression of service, my worst impression was like at Fort Bragg. We were fighting like the Civil War all over again, all the officers and all the noncoms or Southerners. And they hated us white crackers, you know, and all that crap. I fought a little Golden Gloves so I was taking them guys on at night and taking care of them. After a while they kept away from me.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: So when did you go into the service then?

sp.speaker: Sam Edward Buemi
sp.p: That was in -- yeah --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Approximately. I don't need an exact date.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Oh, so it was before the attack on Pearl Harbor?

sp.speaker: Sam Edward Buemi
sp.p: No, wait a minute, wait a minute. No, it was '42, that's right.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: That would be '42, right? Okay.

sp.speaker: Sam Edward Buemi
sp.p: Yeah. After Pearl Harbor, looked like a few months went by and boom, I was gone. Like I say, for me it was a little vacation.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: So what other stories do you remember from your training time?

sp.speaker: Sam Edward Buemi
sp.p: Well, the training time, like I say, I got into Fort Bragg, North Carolina, and they just hated us Northerners. And I was with the 9th Infantry Division and that was a New York State National Guard outfit, I believe, 9th Infantry. And these guys were all shoits [phonetic] and do this and do that, and it was like a new language. And I don't know. I met some good guys in there. In fact, one of them I have to thank for my life. He did save my life at one time at a base in Africa. But okay, that's that training at Bragg. I was having all kinds of problems there because, like I say, I was Northern, they was Southerners and they was fighting the Civil War all over. And I had quite a few problems there. But then after we got to know each other and all of that, guys turned out to be pretty good, you know. Then when we made the invasion in Africa, I come up __+ all loaded with ammo, loaded for beer because I figured, you know, if I got to get killed, I'm going to take something with me, you know. And ironically a wave hit me and knocked me over. I couldn't get up out of the water. But I was loaded. I had a Thompson, I had a Browning Automatic and I had a Side Iron 45 and loaded with ammo. And this one guy, Frank Londotti from New York, he stopped me. He stopped me, he helped me up on my feet. And they were shooting at us from a cliff because, you know, because the invasion, we come in Safi, Africa and we come in and hit a cliff. And actually it was about 200, 300 yards in was the cliff and they were up on the cliff shooting down at us. And anyway, I got out of that water and made it over to the cliff. They couldn't shoot straight down. So, you know, anyway, we ended up getting up on top and chasing them all over the place.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Was this about what, fall, '42?

sp.speaker: Sam Edward Buemi
sp.p: '42, like latter part of -- November 8th was the invasion so it was November. And while we were at Kasserine Pass or something in Africa, I run across Patton twice, and he didn't care whether -- like he wanted us to take a hill, and he says, I don't give a damn how many men you get killed, I want that hill. And he was right there by my hole talking, you know, him and Colonel Randall. Colonel Randall was our company commander at the time. And we had to take the hill because there's maybe about 40 or 50 tanks out in the field; they're all burning. Them Germans were knocking them tanks out like you won't believe. Now, I actually saw a crew set up a 37-millimeter anti-tank weapon, a 37, and shooting at the German tanks, and the shells were just bouncing off of the tank. Then these guys jumped in the hole because the tank came at them and they ground them down and it started rotating around and around over the hole and buried -- killed these guys. I witnessed that. But then after Kasserine, they called for volunteers to help the British going up Sofax (ph). I can't even remember the towns there in Africa. And we traveled, I don't know, about two or three nights, and we got to them and we made an attack. We were on the left flank in order to prevent Germans from surrounding them while we were in the attack, and we were in the middle of everything. We were getting shot and killed at. But the one thing I remembered, I never will forget it, we had these Germans on the run. I mean, we were really kicking them in the butt. And they were -- all of a sudden we stopped, and I asked the sergeant, I said, what in the hell is this, let's go, you know. He said tea time. What do you mean tea time? Son of bitches, they stop for tea right in the middle of combat, stop for tea. I couldn't believe it, you know. So then the ironic part of everything, this guy that plays the bagpipes.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Sam Edward Buemi
sp.p: He gets up and I guess he started blowing his bagpipes, let the Germans know they're coming, right, those dumb, stupid idiots. I don't know how them British -- you know. But anyway, we spent about -- I think about six or seven days with them, and then they pulled us off because we had them on the run pretty good, and we had got back to outfit and getting into Bizerte in Africa. And then it was all over but the shouting in Africa. Then we went into Sicily, made the invasion of Sicily. And Sicily is nonplus like. We were shot at a few times, but everybody was running. No, but Sicily was over, I'd say, in about a month. I got into an argument with my company commander, and 9th Infantry was supposed to go to England for R and R, and what had happened is my company commander told me to take my squad and take that hill and I told him get his ass out of the hole and let's go, you know. And he said you don't talk to me like that. And I said, I'll talk to you any God damned way I wanted to, you know. He started to go for his gun and I had a Browning Automatic shoulder, but at the time I took divisional honors in the Browning Automatic. I could shoot that weapon.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: So that was your job with the outfit, the BAR man?

sp.speaker: Sam Edward Buemi
sp.p: BAR man, yeah. And he says, Buemi, I'm getting you killed. I said, Well, I got news for you, pal. You better watch your ass. And I walked away from him. Now, he was a captain, Captain -- I don't want to mention his name. He's dead anyway, but -- Anyway, I was in the -- because of battalion, I was in all patrols, combat patrols, recomb patrols and all of that. And they tried to get me killed I think. But I was lucky. Everybody else around me was getting killed but me.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Do you have any specific memories of any of those patrols?

sp.speaker: Sam Edward Buemi
sp.p: Yeah. I was taking these guys out all the time and bringing them all back. You know, like a lot of guys, they go out on patrol and a guy get killed and they leave them, but we bring them back. And they gave me a Bronze Star for that, for bringing all the guys back all the time, but --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: You were losing guys fairly regularly when you went out on patrol?

sp.speaker: Sam Edward Buemi
sp.p: Well, ironically maybe one or two. I remember a couple times we, while out on combat patrol -- no, it was a recomb patrol -- and we just lost it. A guy stepped out of line and stepped on the Bouncing Betty and two or three guys got killed on that. But you can hear the pop when the bouncing Betty pops up out of the ground. Are you familiar with them?

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: I'm familiar. I've heard about them, yes.

sp.speaker: Sam Edward Buemi
sp.p: Yeah. Well, you step on them, they bounce up out of the ground and blow about three foot up, four foot up, and they take out a nice circle of guys, you know. And we lost a few men that way. They were always told step in the next guy's path, you know, don't step out of line. We were walking in like four or five inches of water in a stream like and this guy stepped out of line and stepped right on a booby trap. But anyway -- but we had a lieutenant, we went out on the recomb patrol when -- where the hell was that, in Africa or Sicily or Italy or what? No, that was in Africa. That was -- no, that had to be in Italy. We went out on a combat patrol and everybody was -- either that Thompson or Browning or not a lot of power. We got to this certain point up on the hill like looking down and we can see the -- like a super highway. We had like crossed this gully and it was a gully with a valley like and then the town was up on the hill. I don't remember the name of the town, but it was like broad daylight. And this lieutenant says, come on, we're going to take this hill. I says you go, you go alone. My men aren't going. So he said, you're going to get me court-martialed and all this crap, you know. So meanwhile, I come down off of the hill and him and I had a subtle -- not subtle argument, but, you know, I told the guy wait till nightfall and then we'll go ahead and check the (counter). We were going to find out how many Germans were in town, see. So while we were down talking to this lieutenant, we had one guy stand watch like, you know. He started hollering and we went up there and here comes German tanks and trucks full of Germans. We would have we been caught out in the open and we would have been slaughtered out there. So anyway, he apologized. He didn't exactly apologize. He said, forget the court-martial. I told him, No kidding. But that night we went up in the town and I run across some woman that spoke real good American and Italian and she said no Germans were there, they had left two, three days ago. So we radioed in, we have the town. So they came up and we went from there. I'm trying to think, was that Sicily or was that Italy?

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: So you never did get that rest in England, in Sicily?

sp.speaker: Sam Edward Buemi
sp.p: No, no. I went continuous combat. I spent about two and a half years steadily in combat.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Where did you land when you invaded Italy?

sp.speaker: Sam Edward Buemi
sp.p: Salerno.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Sam Edward Buemi
sp.p: At -- Sicily was (Shipfalu) I don't know where the hell we went in there, Sicily, but Salerno, this was -- we were -- oh, I was transferred to the 3rd Infantry, from 9th Infantry, 9th Infantry went to England. 3rd Infantry was going into combat in Italy so I was transferred into Italy into the 3rd Infantry as a BAR man. No, you know what I did? I got rid of that gun and I grabbed a rifle. That sucker was heavy, you know. I'm a little guy, right? So I run across a friend of mine, and this is ironic, Sam Provalianti (ph), the guy, he died not too long ago. We were -- when he transferred me to 3rd Infantry to the 9th, I went to like a repple depple, a redeployment outfit, and Patton was there giving a speech and everybody was standing at attention or standing up, you know, at ease. And I went and I laid down under trees asleep, get some shut-eye while this guy was with his mouth talking. And I got kicked in the foot. A guy tells me -- lieutenant. He looked down, told me, Get up, get in line. I told him get the hell out of -- you know, hit the road. And I went back to sleep. But then I heard some guys say boy, that guy looks just like that guy I know back home, Bill Buemi, you know. Sam Provalianti. So he was slated to go -- I think there was a 45th Infantry. He just came in from the States and I was going to the 3rd Infantry. So I just told him, just get your bag and come with me. He says, I'm supposed to go over there. Get your bag and come with me. So we went back and we got aboard a truck, go to 3rd Infantry. Then I saw the first sergeant there and I told him, this guy is named Sam Provalianti. He's supposed to be at the 45th, but he's coming with me. He's my neighbor and he was my neighbor here in Cleveland. They asked me what I was. I said I'm a rifleman. So they give me a rifle and they give -- they give -- I think they give Sam a rifle at the time, but they called him and then he comes back with a Browning Automatic. So I go up to this first sergeant and I tell them, You stupid asshole, you don't give that ass- -- he don't know his ass from his elbow about that gun. He said, Well, somebody got to be a BAR man. You handle it then if you don't want him to handle it. So I went back to being a BAR man. When Sammy got wounded then I didn't see him anymore. But that was -- then up in Italy, we went through all the Monte Casino, the whole bit. We tried taking that hill about three or four times and we couldn't do it. Then we got the orders to pull back about ten miles back past the Garigliano River, and that's when the planes come over, the bombers. Thousands of them things in my mind anyway, bombing the Monte Casino. Then right after the bombing we tried to take the hill again; we couldn't take the hill. And before I know it, they pulled us back. And I said, Man, we're going to get some rest over here, you know, finally. Anyway, pulled us back and loaded up our LSD's and maintenance, Anzio, and that was slaughter. That was also -- the beach was about 14 miles deep. There were towns in between, small areas with different names, but there's, I think, 22 miles wide and about 14 miles deep. And we went in there and somehow or another -- I don't know how the hell it happened -- we got two Jeeps and we took off and went through the Ringer Mountains (ph) in the town of Cisterna, I think it was called, and there were no Germans there so we called in, come on up, you know. We got the town of Cisterna. And this asshole, I think his name was General Evans, I don't know. Anyway, the general says come back to the beach. And I didn't want to go back to no beach. I had been up there alone. The sergeant told Me, Come on, we got to pull out. We got to go back to the beach. I don't know how many guys got killed trying to take that town of Cisterna after that, but that lasted about three or four months trying to tack in and taking the town. Couldn't do it. The Germans found out we were there and they came in and they throw, if I remember, around eight or nine divisions around us there, and they shot leaflets at us. I got some leaflets downstairs that I got from Anzio, and --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Leaflets to try to get you to surrender?

sp.speaker: Sam Edward Buemi
sp.p: Yeah. I remember one of them. They gave us such and such a time to surrender during the -- bush us (ph) during the bush us and drown us like rats, bush us, ocean or sea, whatever the hell it was, and --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Was the resistance pretty stiff when you first landed at Anzio?

sp.speaker: Sam Edward Buemi
sp.p: No, no. We caught these guys on the beach drunk and laying broads and whatnot, and all through the beach, and when we got the Jeep, a little after that, these guys went into hotels and caught these guys naked in the hotels. That was an R and R area for the Germans, this Anzio Beach down below Rome. And no resistance at all. I don't think a shot was -- I don't even think they knew we were there. We walked in there -- now, what stupid idiot would invade below Rome? You know, you go above Rome, but I think our purpose was to make this invasion at Anzio, then shoot across to Monte Casino or something, some place in there, and try to get them Germans off of Monte Casino is what I think what they had in mind. Never happened. Lost a lot of men there. But anyway, them numbers -- that one I will never forget, we took the town, they told us go back to the beach. That was like shooting monkeys in a barrel, that Anzio Beach, bitch. But then I was wounded at a place called Puncturatio (ph) at Anzio. It was just a little thing there.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Tell me about that, when you were wounded.

sp.speaker: Sam Edward Buemi
sp.p: Well, they called me in, they called me in the office, and they said they're going to give me a battlefield commission. I was the only guy left like in the company. Well, not that bad, there were a few guys, few of us left. And I told them they can stick it. All I'm trying to do is get the hell out of here alive, you know. And got some coffee there, then I went back and it was all mud. I mean, that's what saved my life, the mud, because the shell came over, landed behind me, hit me in the leg, shrapnel. And during the night we come out of the hole because it's full of water, you know. But we had one incident there where I was on -- I was on the forward listening post with two other guys. I remember this one guy's name was Blanchard. I can't remember the other guy, but the water, we were guarding like on a point and there was like a stream and they ride right where we were. And I went back -- I went back into -- they called me into something, I don't know, maybe a staff sergeant or some damn thing at the time then. And we get a call from -- we didn't get a call, we were listening to a radio, that's right, and it's Sally the Bitch of Berlin.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Right, Axis Sally?

sp.speaker: Sam Edward Buemi
sp.p: Yeah. She was on the line. She says, We just have two men from Company F 15th Infantry. They don't even know where they're gone. I said what? So we shot out there. Of course, we had a crowd of Germans firing at you, you know, why the hell not. Get up there and their belts, their ammo and their helmets were laying there. These Germans -- Now, he called in. That's right, Blanchard called in and he says he hears noise. I tell him don't shoot anybody because we had all kind of patrols out so make sure you get the (passer) before you open fire. We didn't hear no more. And about ten or 15 minutes we hear Sally the Bitch of Berlin, come on this radio. But we went out there. Like I say, there wasn't nothing there, just stuff. They snuck up on these guys, Blanchard. Oh, well. That's about all I can remember other than hitting like -- I got hit from the shrapnel shell and then I ended up -- they give me a shot of morphine when I went back to the CP. The first place I stopped they give me morphine and they put a tourniquet on my leg and put me on the Jeep. And there's shelling all over the damn place, and we made it through to another CP and the guy's ready to give me another shot of morphine. Well, what they do, morphine has a long needle on it. They take this needle and they bend it and they hang it on your shirt to let them know that you already took a shot of morphine, you know. Somehow or another that came off, flopped off of me, right, so I get to this other place, this guy's ready to give me another shot and he give me a shot. I said, How many shots are you guys going to give me, I already took a shot. He said, You did? They were slapping me around and giving me black coffee and walking me around. I couldn't walk, you know, because they gave me an overdose of morphine. But anyway, I lived through that crap. But I don't know.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: How long did you recuperate then from that wound?

sp.speaker: Sam Edward Buemi
sp.p: I spent 11 months in the hospital. My wound was such that if they sewed it, I would have had a limp. They cleaned -- my main artery was shot out, was cut out, was cut, and they give me booster shots to force the blood down into my leg. And damn thing still bugs me, but it's -- I'm just glad to be alive so I don't bitch and moan about nothing, you know. So that 11 months in that hospital, they couldn't sew my wound, it was wide open, and it just had to heal that way. And they kept putting bandages and stuff on it, you know. So I told them, Hey, look, I'd like to have like 30 days, go home, get the hell out of here. So they give me a convalescence leave 30 days. Well, about six months later I got married and I went back to work and --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: That was after that 11 months you took a 30-day leave that never ended?

sp.speaker: Sam Edward Buemi
sp.p: Well, it was like six months. All of a sudden we were in a -- I got to tell you, we stayed in attic rooms that in the winter you wore a coat and gloves to stay in that house. And I'll never forget them God damned days. But anyway, in the summer we used to walk around just in shorts, you know, because it's so hot up there.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Where was that? Was this in Cleveland?

sp.speaker: Sam Edward Buemi
sp.p: It's Cleveland. Now it's on 149th and off of Kinsman in Cleveland. And I paid for like half of the coal and it was always cold, you know. So one day I wanted to take a bath so I wanted to get hot water. Well, they always turned the -- old Italian couple. They owned the house. They lived downstairs. They -- I turned the hot water tank on and I went upstairs, waited like a half hour so I turned the water on. The water was still ice cold, you know. And I thought God damn it, you know. So I go downstairs, the tank was off. I thought what the hell is this? So I figured it blew out, you know. So I lit the tank again, went back upstairs and waited a half hour. Still the water was cold. In fact me, my and wife would do dishes. She used to throw on pot of water on the stove, get it hot and do the dishes. You know, she was like that. So I go back downstairs again, it was off again. So I got upstairs, got a paper, whatever the hell I was reading, I went down the basement and I lit that tank and I stayed down the basement. And here she comes sneaking down, the lady that owned the house. And I told her, You touch that God damned tank, I'll kill you. I said, I'm using my God damned half a coal now and I want this water hot. And I started shoveling coal in there like theses guys on the steam ship you see with the shovels throwing it. That's what I __+. That son of a bitch went in there and pulled the coal out with her hands out of the furnace.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Were your hospital stays mostly stateside those 11 months?

sp.speaker: Sam Edward Buemi
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: You came back pretty soon after you were wounded?

sp.speaker: Sam Edward Buemi
sp.p: I was at three different hospitals.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Three different hospitals stateside?

sp.speaker: Sam Edward Buemi
sp.p: Yeah, Stark General in South Carolina, Percy Jones in Michigan. I think Crile.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Crile in Cleveland?

sp.speaker: Sam Edward Buemi
sp.p: Crile here.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Right. Exactly.

sp.speaker: Sam Edward Buemi
sp.p: Then they shipped me back to -- back to Battle Creek.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: So about when were you wounded approximately, do you remember?

sp.speaker: Sam Edward Buemi
sp.p: March or June.

sp.speaker: Sam Edward Buemi
sp.p: I'm pretty sure it was '44. Yeah, it had to be '44.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: You mentioned that one buddy that was wounded. Did you lose any other buddies over there?

sp.speaker: Sam Edward Buemi
sp.p: Oh, yeah. Oh, God, every day I lost guys, you know. My first -- my first baptism in fire was when we were in Africa. We were like -- what the hell do they call that? We were to be used at -- they run across -- somebody up front runs across a lot of fire, they would throw us in there to help them out, and we were going like back and forth and around and across and all that. And we were supposed to be behind the lines, right, maybe a mile or so and we were surrounded. The Germans had us surrounded. And this guy next to me, Joe Crupa was his name, he got hit direct in the back with a mortar shell. I had blood all over me and all of it from him. And meanwhile, we're hollering, Let's get the hell out of here, you know, let's go, you know. They were just shooting the hell out of us, you know, machine gun fire and mortar shells and all of that. We got up -- well, this -- going up this one hill, I don't know. It was on an angle, like toward the right, and then the left was another hill the Germans were on and they could see us going up this hill and they were shooting at us from one hill to the next hill. And that's when Otto Knecht got wounded, Hugh Hatrick -- Hugh Hatrick got wounded. I didn't get wounded at the time. I -- I had -- I had a shrapnel wound in Africa, but it was just a slight -- slight cut like, you know. And I had a medic come up to me and he says -- he was taking care of me while there are all kind of guys hollering mama and all of that. I thought go take care of these guys, I can handle this. So I had the __+ in the pack. I put it on there with a bandage. I took care of myself. That was awful.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: So that day you said you were surrounded, was that basically your first day in combat, or do you have specific memories of the first time somebody was shooting at you?

sp.speaker: Sam Edward Buemi
sp.p: I say that's the first time, but we were -- we were -- in Africa we were shooting -- in Africa itself, Safi, going around Casablanca, we were -- Casablanca was here and we were down below. We were supposed to surround Casablanca to like stop all officers from coming out, the German officers, and we did do that later, but we were getting shot at a few times by patrols, and the German planes were coming over steadily straight for us and bombing us. We were like the fodder. They were using us as fodder over there, I guess, because they wanted -- they wanted -- Germany quit and all they can get. They gave us orders, any pistol, any rifle, anything, get it because they wanted it. So as we were catching these Germans, we were taking whatever they had on them. I know they found out that 37 millimeter they had wasn't worth shit. That was -- that was no weapon at all. But anyway, that's what we had. That's what we went in with, but --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Did you have any encounters with civilians, either in Africa or Sicily or Italy?

sp.speaker: Sam Edward Buemi
sp.p: Yeah, but, you know, they were after the Americans, you know. Americans are all rich no matter what. I saw an incident where -- what the hell was that about now in Africa? Oh, this guy got his ass beat. He was trying to sell stuff at a corner and he was like charging me about ten times as much, and this French officer come up to me and clubbed that guy, beat the shit out of him, you know. Speaking of French now, there was the Gurkhas and the Senegalese and they attached like about six of them to our outfit in combat and these guys were black-black. I mean, you couldn't see them at night. But good fighters.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: I heard the Gurkhas were pretty brutal, right?

sp.speaker: Sam Edward Buemi
sp.p: Yeah. I have a Gurkha knife. I brought it back from Africa. When I come home from -- I was in the hospital in Italy, then they transferred me back over to Africa and that's where I boarded a ship in Africa to come back home. And that's where I picked up this -- you ever seen one of them Gurkha knives?

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Kind of a --

sp.speaker: Sam Edward Buemi
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Sam Edward Buemi
sp.p: Yeah, exactly. I got it on the fireplace.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Was there a lot of souvenir collecting in the outfit?

sp.speaker: Sam Edward Buemi
sp.p: I don't know. I have this knife, and when I was wounded we had -- we had like three or four guys in each bag of -- barracks bag. Rather than have like three or four barracks bag, all put it in like one. Whatever we had, had to cut it down so it would fit into one bag. We cut the number of bags to handle and all of that crap. And I had -- the guy kept a diary all through Africa and I still have one. It's downstairs though, Italy, where it gives you the code word, the date on the radio because we had to talk back and forth, you know, and I don't know how the hell I got it, but I got to be a radio man.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: When did that happen?

sp.speaker: Sam Edward Buemi
sp.p: I don't know. I have no idea.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Was this when they finally let you put the BAR down or did you have to do that too?

sp.speaker: Sam Edward Buemi
sp.p: I think I carried the Browning Automatic all the time. As a lieutenant, Lieutenant -- what the hell was his name? They had a Browning Automatic shoot-out in Africa after the campaign was over and all of that, and they had like all the Browning Automatic men from 9th Infantry. There must have been 50 guys, you know, and you set up different targets and -- anyway, I came out number one. My name was on top as being the top gunner, Browning Automatic gunner. And every target you had to set like your distance. And I was doing pretty good. But anyway, this lieutenant says he wanted me to be his bodyguard with a Browning Automatic. Well, all the lieutenants had a bodyguard. So I was -- Ray Larson. Damn it, how could I forget it. Ray Larson, Lieutenant Ray Larson.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: You didn't --

sp.speaker: Sam Edward Buemi
sp.p: I was his bodyguard.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: You were his bodyguard then?

sp.speaker: Sam Edward Buemi
sp.p: Well, his bodyguard. I dug a hole and said, Hey, Ray, you know. I called him Ray, him and I, but with other guys around, lieutenant, you know. He was a good guy. He got killed. Ray Larson.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Other than tea time, did you get along with the British soldiers?

sp.speaker: Sam Edward Buemi
sp.p: No.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Did you spend time with them?

sp.speaker: Sam Edward Buemi
sp.p: No, never cared for them. No, that made an impression on me I'll never forget. Stop in combat. You got these guys on the run, you stop like a dummy for tea? I hate tea. I used to drink tea. I will not touch tea, not for __+. Want some tea? No, get the hell away from me. I just got that in my mind, tea.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Remember mail call, getting packages from home, that sort of thing?

sp.speaker: Sam Edward Buemi
sp.p: Yeah, I got a package of spam. Yeah, it was ironic, but you know what? We had cans were C Rations, right? I got to a point eating them C Rations morning, noon and night every day for a long time to the point where I opened up a can of the C Rations just from the smell and I throw up. After I throw up, I eat whatever was in there. But they were bad. Fresh meat, where the hell did I kill that cow? Me and Hugh Dunlop, Hugh Dunlop, he's from Detroit, Michigan. I think he's still alive, Hugh. We were -- no, it wasn't Africa. I think it was in Sicily. Spotted this cow so I told Hugh, I said, we're going to kill this son of a bitch and bring it back. We're going to have some God damned meat, you know. So I downed him with the Browning and we go to get him. We dragged that son of a bitch, must have been three miles we dragged that cow over to this tent. Never forget this cook's name. His name was Gordon. We used to call him Flash Gordon. And I told him I want a steak two inches thick, you know, and I don't give a shit. Do what you want with all this meat, we want steaks. And there was eight or nine of us then. He says, Okay, he says, I'll get it all ready. We went to eat and we have stew, you know. Well, the stew was like -- we had stew in the cans as far as that goes. If I get this God damned Gordon, I'm going to kill him. The way this guy went over the hill, he grabbed all this God damned meat and he went into town for some broads and took the meat with him. We never saw him no more. Never saw him anymore. He took the cheap meat and took off. I never got that damn steak. But I will say that I don't know what they're eating today in the service, but you -- C Rations, and maybe once a month is okay, but not every day morning, noon and night every day for months. And I went in with good teeth, I mean, my teeth, I could bite nails. I come out all bleeding. I had to take them all out and I had to put it to that, the food, maybe even taking a bath. Who knows, take a bath. They lost me a few times because I had welts all over my body from fleas and all that crap.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Did you write home much? Did you get a chance?

sp.speaker: Sam Edward Buemi
sp.p: I wrote home all the time.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: What kinds of things would you write about?

sp.speaker: Sam Edward Buemi
sp.p: You want to see what I was writing about?

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Sure. Yeah.

sp.speaker: Sam Edward Buemi
sp.p: Let me get that album out there. I made that up.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: That's very nice.

sp.speaker: Sam Edward Buemi
sp.p: These are all the organizations I belong to.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Sam Edward Buemi
sp.p: That's a piece of shrapnel that I carried. I carried it around with me, yeah.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Is that the one you dug out of the --

sp.speaker: Sam Edward Buemi
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: -- little piece from Africa?

sp.speaker: Sam Edward Buemi
sp.p: No, that was at Anzio.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: That was at Anzio?

sp.speaker: Sam Edward Buemi
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: So you got hit a few times, just the last time was the most serious, right?

sp.speaker: Sam Edward Buemi
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: You didn't get a chance to get close to any of these other generals, did you, Mark Clark and General Bradley?

sp.speaker: Sam Edward Buemi
sp.p: I seen them. I seen them a few times, but nothing talk to. Now, Patton I seen around four times and so it was Wes Moreland. Of course, Wes Moreland was after. I saw him at a reunion. I saw Wes Moreland at Bragg, at Fort Bragg. But him and I got along real good. In fact, I have a picture downstairs of him and I.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Oh, yeah?

sp.speaker: Sam Edward Buemi
sp.p: Yeah, the letters.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Now, as far as Patton, you were close enough to hear what he was saying?

sp.speaker: Sam Edward Buemi
sp.p: Oh, yeah.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: But he wasn't talking to you at all?

sp.speaker: Sam Edward Buemi
sp.p: No, he wasn't talking to me. No, he wasn't talking to me. Let me look at this. I haven't seen this in -- let me look at it.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Sam Edward Buemi
sp.p: 9th Infantry, 3rd Infantry.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: These letters were written from Africa, Tunisia, Sicily, Italy, Anzio Beachhead to my wife and parents. You were dating at the time, I assume. Your wife was your fiancée?

sp.speaker: Sam Edward Buemi
sp.p: Yeah, yeah, yeah. We've been married 59 years now.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Do you remember what your reunion was like when you finally got back to the states? That was probably in the hospital I assume?

sp.speaker: Sam Edward Buemi
sp.p: No, I was walking around with a cane at the time. I haven't looked in that thing in years. Oh, you know, I should have got that propaganda stuff.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Oh, yeah.

sp.speaker: Sam Edward Buemi
sp.p: Yeah. This is the propaganda stuff. These are just copies. They shot these over when we're at the beachhead and --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: I should say that out loud so we can hear it on the tape. The one leaflet says, Rich Man's War, Poor Man's Fight. Those are fascinating.

sp.speaker: Sam Edward Buemi
sp.p: Yeah. Them things fell apart on me.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: So they dropped these, drop these just --

sp.speaker: Sam Edward Buemi
sp.p: They issue in a shell they'd blow and these leaflets would all come out or the plane would come over. I did have the opportunity of waving to the German pilot though.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Oh, yeah?

sp.speaker: Sam Edward Buemi
sp.p: When we were at Anzio Beach, they'd come over the mountain and come right down almost -- I tell you, 15, 20 feet above the beach, and then they'd drop a bomb on the beach and a skid bomb __. I'll tell you, them German pilots were good. But anyway, this guy come over and I was sitting on the edge of the hole. I didn't know what the hell he was until I saw the Swastika on the tail, and I waved like this and he waved back. I'll never forget that.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Oh, man. That's amazing.

sp.speaker: Sam Edward Buemi
sp.p: But that was a shot -- a shot out of a million, I guess, seeing a German guy coming because he was coming down and he was skip bombing and there was a lot of ships out there burning at Anzio.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Any other little stories like that that you remember or --

sp.speaker: Sam Edward Buemi
sp.p: Yeah, there's a lot of them. I can't put them together though or another half hour, whatever it is.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Right. Exactly.

sp.speaker: Sam Edward Buemi
sp.p: Yeah, those.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: So did you say when you saw your fiancée, soon to be your wife, for the first time, it was in the hospital then or when you got back?

sp.speaker: Sam Edward Buemi
sp.p: No. When I -- I know right from -- right from the ship I was sent to Stark General in South Carolina.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Sam Edward Buemi
sp.p: And I was there maybe about 30 days, and I started moaning about I wanted to get close to home so they sent me to Battle Creek, Michigan and that's when -- no, I got married -- we were married then. She came -- she stayed with us. Well, she stayed in town with some people that had a room for rent or something. Real nice people. Damn it, I forget their names though. They were real nice to my wife and I.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: When you were overseas, did you get any shows or anything like that, any chance to review --

sp.speaker: Sam Edward Buemi
sp.p: I never got to see anything. As a matter of fact, a man from U.S.O. come up with donuts I think about 20 miles back. You guys want donuts, come on, let's go. We had to march maybe ten miles. I said 20, but I'd say ten miles behind the line. Figured they could take the donuts and stick it. Bring it up here. I never got any of those frills or anything like that.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Did you guys ever do anything to make your own entertainment?

sp.speaker: Sam Edward Buemi
sp.p: Oh, wait a minute. I was -- where the hell was it? I was up in Italy and they finally come up to my hole and they says, You got five days combat leave to go into Naples, all right. Now, they got me out of the hole, let me -- first I got deloused, the very first thing. Got rid of all my clothes. I had a beard on me like about three, four inch beard and shaved, cleaned up, got deloused, got another uniform on and all that. And before I left there was around five guys that are still on the line and they knew I was going back and they knew that they didn't have the combat time I had and they didn't know whether they were ever going to get off that line. So about five of them give me money, who gave me 50 bucks, who gave me a hundred bucks, you know, and they give me their names and addresses at home here and said buy something and send it and write a little letter out and doing okay and all of this junk. So I got that money, went into town, got deloused and changed uniforms and all of that. And I'm looking in the windows and they had like -- I'm Italian. They got a price for soldiers and a price for Italians, right. So anyway, I see this pretty girl. Man, she was pretty, walking down the street in Naples, and I stopped her. And I talk a little Italian. I told her I had a problem. I got to buy this stuff for friends of mine and I'd like to have her give me a hand to help buy this stuff. And she says she got time. So she comes into the store with me and she started ranting and raving, talking to these people about this is my cousin and you don't charge him that kind of money, all that stuff, half the price or whatever the hell they had marked there, you know. And we made up all those packages and went into the post office and made them up, and wrote out the addresses and a little letter with each package and mailed them to all these guys -- to their parents. And I told her -- she said she had someplace to go and I thought I'd like to meet her later so she told me a street and place and we shacked up together. Hey, I figured I'm getting killed any damn way. But this was then. I was a single -- single person. She was a pretty girl. Tina somebody or another. I can't remember her last name. But you know what? Let me go back now where the hell was I at? Yeah, I was in the hospital. Sammy Provalianti. I told you him and I were buddies and he got wounded. And he was on the hospital staff. So I get wounded and Sam __ is taking me to the hospital and I told his driver, By the way, I says, I think I have a buddy of mine that's -- I don't know what the hell, shot in a million, Sam Provalianti. Sam? Yeah, we know Sam, you know. I thought you tell him where I'm at. Fine, we'll look him up and we'll tell you. So about two days later here comes Sam with oranges and apples and all this crap. So I told him, you know what, you hear of Tina Little (ph)? Bring her back here. So I didn't see the guy no more. Guy took off.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: With Tina?

sp.speaker: Sam Edward Buemi
sp.p: With Tina. Later I thought we come home all wounded, come home and got out of the hospital and I see Sammy and I happened to mention, I says, Hey, Sammy, whatever happened to the time I told you I had to get Tina, get her in the hospital so I can get laid and all this? He said she was so good I stayed with her. My buddy. My buddy. Sammy was a great guy. He died not too long ago, maybe about four years ago, five years ago. We were going out together, his wife, Stella. Nice girl and --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: What did you think about your experiences during the war? Does one particularly vivid memory come to mind?

sp.speaker: Sam Edward Buemi
sp.p: Yeah, keep out of the infantry. Look like I tried so damn hard to get the hell out of that infantry. But then again, you know, I was telling you about this girl, Tina. We went into Naples and this and that and we were shacking up and my five days was up, I got to go back to camp. And she told me her brother -- oh, she introduced me to her brother. Her brother's my size, put his clothes on this and that, I'll be a civilian. She said you speak Italian this and that so you stay with us, stay here. I couldn't do it. I couldn't it, no. So I jumped out of bed one morning like five six or o'clock in the morning and I left. I told her good-bye. Then I got on the line, I thought about how crazy I was to do that. I should have stayed with her, but that's the way that goes.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Did you try to get a transfer out of the infantry to anywhere else?

sp.speaker: Sam Edward Buemi
sp.p: That's why I volunteered for these other things. I don't know, I volunteered for so God damned many combat patrols recomb patrols, the First Special Services forces was giving up a bunch of guys to go around and see what the hell these Germans were doing. There was -- yeah, what the hell was that about? I don't know. I figured I'd get the hell out of this infantry. But that was worse. I was in there and what was his name? Damn. But anyway, we got around -- we were watching these Germans do pulse order drill, calisthenics and all of this stuff. We were watching that while we were tearing up their wiring and all of that stuff. We went back and disrupted all the wire lines and then when it was all over, it's about 50, 80 of us. Not too many for combat patrol. And I know not too many of us come back. We got in a couple firefights there and I know I made it back. But I thought about that. Didn't think too much about it. They give me a little pin like an asp on it. We were supposed to be here and we were like 40 miles away. The Germans, we were behind them. General Truscott, yeah General Truscott was in charge of 3rd Infantry division and we were -- everybody had a bear and -- who the hell had shaven? Who had shaven? Never saw a razor in months. But they passed out razors and all of that to shave and looked like new troops and we were going to fool the Germans, new troops coming in. Same old guys, the same old beards and old guys. So we were in front of them Germans and we were going to surround them and like we had to march that night. We would like run and walk like 40 miles in a matter of, I think, four or five hours, we were there. The Germans never knew it. They thought we were in front. We were right on their ass. And we started scaling in and we had a little fight, we cleaned the lines out, then we went and made a good advance on that. But never forget that Truscott Trott. That general always says the way we run and walk, half run, half walk. Fast pace. General Truscott, he's there someplace. I never saw that guy either. Where the hell was Truscott at? He's around here some God damned place. Oh, here it is. Here. Casino. Man, I ain't looked at this thing in a long time.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Yeah, I did one of those with my dad's stuff.

sp.speaker: Sam Edward Buemi
sp.p: I got a good conduct with a question mark. But I'll tell you what, I got in more God damned fights over there, I just did.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Fights with other guys, with officers, or other enlisted men?

sp.speaker: Sam Edward Buemi
sp.p: We had a certain -- are you talking about little incidents. We went into town, me and Hoppy Hopkins and Al Monitor. Hoppy Hopkins's father was something to do with the state government. Now, he was a treasurer or some God damned thing, Hopkins. That name sound familiar?

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Sam Edward Buemi
sp.p: Anyway, that was his son. I told him, Man, you must have been a real fuckup to be on the line there and your father's a big shot in Washington, you know. But we went into town and we had a few drinks and Hoppy got drunk. And so Al Monitor's on one side and I'm on the other side. We're holding Hoppy and we're going back to camp and we pass this lieutenant. He was a 90-day wonder, second Louie, I think. And he said, Soldiers, halt, you know, after we passed him by. What the hell is your problem, you know. And he goes, Don't you salute an officer? I said, Can't you see us, we're holding our buddy up. Don't you salute an officer? I hit this son of a bitch. I hit him, I knocked him down and we took off. We get back to camp. Now, this is like two o'clock in the morning, somewhere around in there, right. Hoppy jumps into his -- we had little pup tents. He jumped into his, I went into mine and so on, so forth. Before we know it, the bugler is out there bugling, everybody fall out. This lieutenant is looking for me or Hoppy or Al Monitor. And I stayed in the tent. I didn't come out. And Hoppy stayed in the tent. He was drunk anyway. This lieutenant, everybody was standing there at attention. He was going up and down the line looking for me. So then lot of us, when Larson come up and he said, Buemi, what the hell happened? So I told him. And he said, This asshole here wanted me to salute him. I'm holding Hoppy and all of that shit and I'll salute him. I hit him. So Larson walked away from me. Didn't say nothing. That's the one that's --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: You must have been a good soldier for them to overlook that kind of stuff?

sp.speaker: Sam Edward Buemi
sp.p: Combat, I was a combat man, and civilian life, hey, a combat man. So many incidents like that happened. I remember I went into town in Africa and ordered a beer and it gets hot. No refrigeration in Africa, you know. Then I ordered -- some guys at the bar, I ordered a drink and they had like a drink and a little glass. You put your little finger in the God damned thing, you know. I said give me a water glass, I'm a tough guy. I never made it back to camp though. Never made it. There was a brick wall there. I went on the other side of the wall and conked out. But we always went into town with a .45 or something. You're not allowed to have a weapon on you going into town. Well, these God damned J rags, they was killing Americans, they was killing everybody just for their shoes and clothing or what the hell not. You know, it's a -- I keep a .45 under the shirt and go into town, but I never used it though, you know. But I was always armed no matter where we were. But I remember, and I often think about it here, why we don't do something like that. Like they fought a few Germans killed there. Where the hell was that at now? That wasn't in Africa, that was in Italy. They found a few Germans killed. And the Germans came out. But for every German they find killed, they're going to kill five civilians. And that's that date. The next day they're going to kill ten, the next day they're going to kill 20, next day they're going to kill 30 for every German soldier daily. They cut it out. They killed about 20, 30, 50 civilians and finally no more. No more. They didn't find any more Germans then. They were killing these guys on the side or, I guess, underground or whatever. So he -- I saw this guy, Murphy, three times.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Yeah?

sp.speaker: Sam Edward Buemi
sp.p: Yeah. We were up in Italy and he was sitting there eating a biscuit just like everybody else and he says -- no, I asked him. I said, What's your name? He said, My name is Murphy. I said, Oh, you're the guy that got all the God damned medals because there was word that went around, you know. He says, Yeah, but hey, if you're in the position I was in, you'd be the same. And I was in position two, three times. I figured, Well, I'm going to get killed so just do what you got to do. But he was lucky he come out of that stuff. But another time he come looking for me and actually says where's that nut Buemi at? Used to call me Bue in the Army. Where's that nut Bue at? Oh, he's around here someplace though. Guys come back and told me, Oh, they was looking for you.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: And he never caught up with you?

sp.speaker: Sam Edward Buemi
sp.p: Only the one time we sat. We talked maybe about -- I don't think we talked three, five minutes --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Sam Edward Buemi
sp.p: -- the one time. We were in -- not a rest area, but we were getting -- supposed to get hot food.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Sam Edward Buemi
sp.p: God damned stew which I can get out of the cans. They emptied the stew out of the cans and heat it up and that's what we got, same bullshit so --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Was he a pretty nice man?

sp.speaker: Sam Edward Buemi
sp.p: Yeah, to me. He was a little shit. I thought I was way taller than him. They said he was 5'6". That's what I am. And I remember standing up and looking a little down on him. So he had to be like 5'4", 5'5". But he said he was 5'6" unless he had high-heeled boots on. Combat boots are what, about this high I think? They're about like maybe an inch and a half. But he had the same thing. He had the same thing on, you know. What else can I say?

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Anything else come to mind?

sp.speaker: Sam Edward Buemi
sp.p: Man, so many things, I can't remember. Little by little they, you know, spark a light.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Exactly. Well, you live close. If you want to sit down again, we can record more.

sp.speaker: Sam Edward Buemi
sp.p: Yeah, I got your number down on my thing downstairs. You know, I was telling you that up at Anzio I was one time and they got me and they says, Oh, we're going to give you a battlefield commission. I told them, I'm not interested in no battlefield commission, I just want to get my God damned ass out of here, you know, and I left. And when I got back to the hole is when I got wounded. That's the way it goes. I don't believe I ever run -- in all my doings with these -- I belong to the VFW, the VAV, the American Legion Combat Veterans, Italian-American Combat Veterans.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Sam Edward Buemi
sp.p: I belong to 14 of them. There's Company F, 15th Infantry. Company F has one, 9th Infantry, 3rd Infantry. There's 14 of them and I haven't run across anybody that were in five invasions, all this crap.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Right. Exactly.

sp.speaker: Sam Edward Buemi
sp.p: And I talked to guys that were in Africa and guys that were in Sicily and Italy, but one guy that was in the Army Air Corp. I think he was in Africa and Sicily.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: He was Air Corp?

sp.speaker: Sam Edward Buemi
sp.p: Yeah, the Air Corp. But I tell you that was so gratifying to see bar plane come over. When you see these German planes coming over, they came and they striked us one time, five planes. They came down and striked us and put a whole column of trucks on fire. And we were like two, 300 yards spread out on both sides of the road firing at these planes. And we knocked four of them down. I went up to the one plane, saw a guy, part of the rib cage blew when he hit the ground. Hell of a hole in that ground. They hit the ground. That will teach you to screw around with us infantry men.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Sam Edward Buemi
sp.p: But it was so gratifying to see an American plane come over. I watched a God damned dog fight down below me, that's how high up in the mountains we were. We were coming around this mountain and ironically there's a company down there firing pulfers (ph), and every time a German plane come around they'd open up at the plane. And we're on this hill, real nice, getting shot at, fired on, pulfers, right? I'll never forget that. The German planes would come around and the American planes would come around. Then the German planes would come around and the American planes would come around. Every time it come around you'd get the hell out of here, get on the other side of this thing. We had that happen in Africa too. We went on an attack and we had a Green and Baldy Hill. I forget what numbers they had. But I noticed the North Star was exactly right over this Green and Baldy Hill. So no matter where we're going, as long as we're going toward the North Star, we're in good shape, right? So we get to a certain point there and this lieutenant -- it wasn't Larson, it was some other lieutenant. He said, Dig in. And I told him, I said, We're digging in on a forward side of the mountain. We got to go on the back side of the mountain. He said, Dig in right here. I'll tell you what. You dig in right here. I'm taking my men, we're digging in on the other side. So I called my men, we went on the hill, up over the hill to the other side. Come day, them Germans spotted -- always raining in combat, always raining in combat. They had their green covers, like covers the hole or something, and shine like light and the Germans saw this and they opened up on these guys. Before I know it, they all come around here. The lieutenant says, You were right. I told him, you're God damned North Start was over the Green and Baldy hill. Couple guys got killed. But like I say, a lot of little incidents like stupidity like that one at Anzio where we took the hill, we go back to the beachhead, assholes, British tea kind bullshit. I'm still here to talk about it, so --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Sam Edward Buemi
sp.p: But you know what, I can't remember who the hell was with me? Well, we got this thing on?

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Sam Edward Buemi
sp.p: Is it got an incident. You got to laugh your ass off about this. In this five days that I got leave in combat, I run across -- his name was -- son of a bitch, how could I forget his name? Morrisinski (ph), called him Morris. Morris and I, they give us a ticket to go get laid because they had the whorehouses at -- like I say, examine the girls and all of this stuff, right. So we'd go into the place there and it's soldiers and sailors and lieutenants and all this bullshit. And go around in the one room and there was a dresser drawer and there was a candle, one candle, that's all the light they had in this is one candle, right. So the broad would say -- call a number, whatever the hell it was, like you're at the PX shopping center, whatever the hell it was. Call the number and the guy would go get laid and he left, right? So we had to wait till our number got called. But every time a girl come out of the room, she'd go to this dresser drawer, put money in there, close the drawer. And she had to like push the money down to close this drawer. So all of a sudden the candle went out and you couldn't see nothing. It was dark, there was scuffling and what the hell not, and then the candle went back, it was maybe about three, four, five minutes. And Morris says Billy, let's go. I said, Well, I want to get laid first. So meanwhile, the madam, the girl come out to put money in there, the money's gone. Somebody snatched all this God damned money, right. So this old lady, she went out on the balcony like one floor up. She hollered, MP, MP, whatever the hell it was, gottivenetti (ph) in Italian would be police. So they come in and Morris and I went over the balcony, jumped off the balcony, we took off because they were locking guys up. So anyway we took off. We run -- we run around a couple miles or so and all of that, then finally we plopped down along side of the building and I said, What kind of son of a bitch would go in and steal all of this money from these broads? He said, I don't know, pulled his zipper down, let's count it. That God damned, Morris. He stole that damn money. That was so funny. At the time I said, You son of a bitch, you stole that money. He said, I don't give a shit. He said, Let's get something to eat now. That was so funny. Morrisinski. Yeah, this guy was good. I don't remember being in combat with him though. I met him on this R and R. He was from a different outfit. Yeah, I had another incident up there at Anzio. We had, like Germans were lighting haystacks. Like we take like a -- maybe a mile away would be a house. We were in one house and a mile away the Germans would be -- not even a mile, about 500 yards, you know. And we'd be shooting back at each other. And they'd be in haystacks and they would be in all kind of haystacks around. And what the hell was happening there? So this one guy was opening up quite a bit with a machine gun. And the haystack he was behind wasn't too far away. So I told the lieutenant -- he was a TD, tank destroyer. That's what he was. And he had a 50-caliber on top of this tank. And I told him, Why don't you wheel that tank around and I'll get this 50 and I'll blast that God damned haystack apart. He says, I'll get out there for a minute or two because they were still shooting. So he come around this building that was called a factory, that place that we were at then. But he had come around with the tank and opened up with this 50 and I set this God damned thing on fire and we backed up. Those Germans, I didn't see no Germans come out of there or anything. I must have thrown a hundred, 200 rounds in that haystack with that 50. But anyway, little incidents, like I say. Then had another time where a guy, new guys, they take two new guys and they put them with old guys, not in age, but in combat.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Right, right, combat.

sp.speaker: Sam Edward Buemi
sp.p: Combat. And this guy grabbed a hand grenade and pulled the pins and what the hell is this, you know. I knocked him on -- I wanted to kill that God damned kid. Got the hand grenade, threw it out of the window of this house we were in. Of course, no roof, no nothing. But there were incidents like that. There were a lot of incidents. I was on forward patrol and there was three of us and I stood my two hours, then you wake the next guy up to stay for two hours and we have the walkie-talkie and if we hear anything we call it in. We're up ahead maybe about a thousand, thousand yards or so. And I'd just sleep with like one eye and the guy that's supposed to be on duty was sound asleep, almost killed him. I beat the shit out of him. Hey, you're supposed to be watching. Little incidents, you know. But -- you know, that's -- you know, after all of that mucking around, here I am. Yeah, but there's an incident here where it was in Africa.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Sam Edward Buemi
sp.p: In Africa, I went over the hill in Africa. And DTC, Disciplinary Training Center. There's some letters in there from there, DTC.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: How long were you there?

sp.speaker: Sam Edward Buemi
sp.p: About a month. No, we went over the hill, me and about five other guys went over the hill in Africa after the Campaign was over and we were getting maimed, blown, screwed, raped, you know. I had a crap game for about 40 grand so I was backing out of the room, borrowed money off -- I figured I was dying anyway so. Damn it. When he says -- we got a flash or something, I don't know who the hell mentioned, going to go into Sicily. So I told the guys, I'm turning myself in, I'm going back to my outfit for Sicily, and if you guys want to turn yourself in, fine. If you want to stay out here, that's okay too. It's up to you guys. So we went and turned ourselves in. They all pulled guns. I said, Hey, we're turning ourselves in. They were MPs, American MPs. So they locked us up. Then they took us to this DTC thing, Disciplinary Training Center. They get up like four in the morning or five in the morning and you go out and march about two miles out in this van in the front. Prisoners all were breaking up rocks, all of that bullshit. Like, you know what it was, our officers, there were Southerners from the Georgia chain gang, so they were like following what they did in Georgia.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Sam Edward Buemi
sp.p: They did it over there. They killed a couple guys in there, these guards. I don't know, just shot them period.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Wow.

sp.speaker: Sam Edward Buemi
sp.p: Now, the paratroopers, they killed a paratrooper in there and one day the paratroopers come by in a Jeep or something, he had some machine guns. Down he goes.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Sam Edward Buemi
sp.p: And they opened up on this guy, this major's tent. That's what it was, Major -- can't remember his damn name either, but he wasn't in. He'd gone into town or something or other. They would have killed him. But they were outside, they were shooting in towards the tent. They riddled that tent with all kind of holes and they took off. But that DTC was something. Desert Training Corp. That's the way -- when I wrote home, I says you'll probably notice on top it says DTC. That's the Desert Training Corp, not the Disciplinary Training Center.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Right. Exactly. And with all that, you got a good conduct medal?

sp.speaker: Sam Edward Buemi
sp.p: Yeah, yeah.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: So when you guys went over the hill, it's just fed up, you just needed a break?

sp.speaker: Sam Edward Buemi
sp.p: Wanted to get food, wanted to get good food because they give us the same bullshit again. We'd been to the area outside of City Bella Bass which is the home of the French Foreign Legionnaires and we went -- we go into town and that's all you see is the French Foreign Legionnaires. And I got the -- God damn it, I got some money still, francs from Africa downstairs. But anyway, this one guy, he was a big sucker. I think he was a Russian though; big. He -- we went in this nightclub. We went in this bar like they had a bar and booze what the hell not, and I told the girl get them guys a drink. There was like four or five of them Legionnaires sitting around. Before they all came over. And one of them spoke Italian like so I speak Italian. So he asked me in Italian if I wanted to have a girl and this and that. What the hell. So they handled -- in Africa they had like medinas which is off -- tabu for American soldiers to go in. That's where all the whores, where the thieves, whatever the hell not, that's where they locked them up. And they had like a French soldier there, a British soldier, an American soldier guarding these gates to make sure nobody goes in there, see. And Hugh Dunlop, he was with me. Yeah, Hugh Dunlop. Anyway, there was a collision. Two command cars somehow or other got in an accident. So these guards lift up both, they run over there. Actually, we shot into the medina, Hugh Dunlop and I. And man, we were running that place. We went and we'd run across that -- that's where we run across some of the French Foreign Legionnaires in there and we had a few drinks with them in there. And this one guy grabbed this girl's leg like this, flipped her up, one arm, one hand, picked this girl up, and stabbed his finger, put it into her, and forget that. But anyway, we filed the -- after they chased us all through the medina and all of that, I was having a good time in between. Then we finally give up. They got us back to our outfit. These two letters were written an hour or two before I was wounded. I was just used to writing two, three, four letters, keep in my knapsack.

sp.speaker: Sam Edward Buemi
sp.p: Is that when the hell it was?

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Sam Edward Buemi
sp.p: Hey, thanks. I didn't know. That's what it says. I don't know whether that guy writes right or not.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: How it happened, it was twilight. Jerry's in the next house 200 yards away. I got out of my --

sp.speaker: Sam Edward Buemi
sp.p: Fox hole.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Yeah, to exercise my legs and to squeeze the water out of my shirt and pants. Jerry spotted me, dropped a mortar shell to keep me company.

sp.speaker: Sam Edward Buemi
sp.p: And here I am. But I said like 500 yards, a thousand yards. There was, like I say, maybe about 200 yards, them houses. And we'd take a house and have it -- well, let's go take that one over there, right. And we go take that one over there and the Germans would go take the ones we just left. They come back, right. So we go back and they shoot us up because we didn't know they done it. Meanwhile, we got a little smarter. We always leave some guys behind and then we'd go take the house. That Anzio was something.
